title: Ezekiel 8:7–13
context: Ezekiel 8:7–13 continues the prophet’s account. The LORD shows him a hole in the wall of the court, tells him to dig, and leads him through a door to see what is done inside (8:7–9). On the walls are portrayed every form of creeping things, unclean animals, and the idols of the house of Israel (8:10). Seventy men of the elders of Israel stand before them with censers, and in their middle stands Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan (8:11). Seventy elders recall the elders who served with Moses (Exodus 24:9; Numbers 11:16), which makes the scene a sharp reversal. Some readers connect this Jaazaniah with the family of Shaphan the scribe, whose son Ahikam appears in 2 Kings 22:12, but the identification is not certain; he is distinct from Jaazaniah the son of Azzur in 11:1. The LORD then quotes the elders’ saying, “The LORD doesn’t see us. The LORD has forsaken the land.” (8:12), which returns in 9:9. The exact nature of the worship depicted is not specified, and these notes describe it soberly without filling in detail the text does not give. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground, holding that hidden idolatry among the leaders, justified by the claim that God neither sees nor cares, stands exposed before him.

verses.text: He brought me to the door of the court; and when I looked, behold, a hole in the wall.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD brings Ezekiel to the door of the court, where he sees a hole in the wall. Arminian readers note that the vision moves from public idolatry to what is hidden, and they see the LORD revealing what the people thought was concealed from him and from others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same movement inward and read it as showing that nothing is hidden from God. They observe that the hole and the door belong to the vision’s symbolic world, and they do not try to locate them precisely in the temple’s architecture.

verses.text: Then he said to me, “Son of man, dig now in the wall.” When I had dug in the wall, I saw a door.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Son of man, dig now in the wall.” When Ezekiel had dug, he saw a door. Arminian readers note that the prophet is made to uncover what is hidden, and they see in this a picture of God’s word exposing secret sin so that it may be recognized and turned from.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same image of uncovering and read it as part of God’s searching judgment, which brings hidden things to light. They observe that Ezekiel’s obedience to a strange command fits the pattern of sign-acts and visions throughout the book.

verses.text: He said to me, “Go in, and see the wicked abominations that they do here.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Go in, and see the wicked abominations that they do here.” Arminian readers note that the prophet is called to witness the people’s sin firsthand, and they see this as preparing him to speak with understanding to the elders who sat before him in exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD names the practices as wicked abominations before Ezekiel sees them, so the verdict is given by God. They read the verse as shared ground on God’s judgment of idolatry, which Ezekiel is shown in order to report it faithfully.

verses.text: So I went in and looked, and saw every form of creeping things, abominable animals, and all the idols of the house of Israel, portrayed around on the wall.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel sees every form of creeping things, abominable animals, and all the idols of the house of Israel portrayed on the wall. Arminian readers note that the images may be of animals unclean under the law, and they read the scene soberly as worship turned toward created things.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same scene and observe that the exact nature of the images is not specified. They read the verse soberly, without filling in details the text does not give, as a picture of worship that exchanges the glory of God for images of creatures.

verses.text: Seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel stood before them. In the middle of them Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan stood, every man with his censer in his hand; and the smell of the cloud of incense went up.
verses.arminianNotes: Seventy elders stood before the images with censers, and in their middle stood Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan. Arminian readers note the echo of the seventy elders of Exodus 24:9 and Numbers 11:16, named without harmonizing, and they see leaders called to serve God now leading in idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same reversal and observe that some connect this Jaazaniah with the family of Shaphan the scribe (compare 2 Kings 22:12), though the link is not certain. They distinguish him from Jaazaniah the son of Azzur in 11:1, and they read the scene as shared ground.

verses.text: Then he said to me, “Son of man, have you seen what the elders of the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in his rooms of imagery? For they say, ‘The LORD doesn’t see us. The LORD has forsaken the land.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Ezekiel what the elders say in the dark: “The LORD doesn’t see us. The LORD has forsaken the land.” Arminian readers note that the elders excuse their idolatry by denying God’s attention and care, and they see this as a turning away rooted in unbelief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same saying and its return in 9:9, named without harmonizing. They read it as revealing the unbelief beneath the idolatry, and they observe the irony that the LORD who sees them in the dark is about to show his departure as a judgment.

verses.text: He said also to me, “You will again see more of the great abominations which they do.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Ezekiel, “You will again see more of the great abominations which they do.” Arminian readers note that the vision builds step by step, and they see in this progression a picture of how idolatry spreads and deepens when it is not confronted and turned from.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same progression and read it as God’s thorough exposure of Judah’s sin. They observe that each scene adds to the case for judgment, and both traditions read the repeated promise of greater abominations as preparing for the climax of the vision.
